title: Cholinergic modulation of error signals

html:
Midbrain dopamine is not the only arbiter of the basal ganglia teaching signal. Once a candidate error reaches the striatum, it enters a dense local cholinergic field generated by cholinergic interneurons (CINs, the classical tonically active neurons (TANs)), whose tonic firing is interrupted by task-locked pauses and rebounds. Recent sensor work further shows that dopamine and acetylcholine are coordinated even outside explicitly rewarded events, implying that the striatal terminal field is not a passive sink for a finished RPE but an active layer that temporally structures how that error is delivered to downstream synapses 1, 2. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Dopamine axons in striatum express nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, so local acetylcholine can act directly on the axon terminal rather than only through cell bodies in the midbrain. Classical work established that endogenous nicotinic cholinergic tone regulates striatal dopamine release, and later optogenetic studies showed that selective activation of CINs is sufficient to evoke dopamine release locally in nucleus accumbens, without requiring a change in midbrain spiking 3, 4. More recent imaging and modeling sharpen this into a circuit principle: single CINs can induce local dopamine release, nicotinic signaling extends the spatial scale over which dopamine spreads, and acetylcholine–dopamine interactions can support traveling waves and mesoscale neuromodulatory structure within striatum 2. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

However, cholinergic modulation is not unidirectionally facilitatory. In dorsal striatum, activation of CINs and axonal nAChRs can impose a short-lived refractory-like suppression on subsequent dopamine release: after nAChR-mediated depolarization, later depolarization events evoke much less dopamine for roughly the next 100 ms, an effect more prominent in dorsal than ventral striatum 5. By contrast, in nucleus accumbens, the same cholinergic interface can amplify the dopamine response to reward when the reward is earned under high effort; blocking this local cholinergic augmentation selectively blunts the enhanced dopamine signal and impairs effortful behavior while sparing low-effort reward consumption 6. The right synthesis is therefore not that acetylcholine simply "adds" or "subtracts" dopamine, but that it supplies a state- and territory-dependent gain control over terminal dopamine output. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The most conceptually important recent result is that acetylcholine also helps determine what the dopamine transient means. In dorsomedial striatum, simultaneous dopamine and acetylcholine measurements during decision-making showed that dopamine supported different computations depending on its phase relationship to cholinergic dynamics 7. When a dopamine RPE slightly lagged a cholinergic dip at the offer cue, it predicted subsequent behavioral updating and trial-to-trial changes in striatal firing, consistent with dopamine-dependent plasticity. When a dopamine transient preceded the cholinergic dip at the reward cue, no comparable relationship to learning was observed. At movement-related events, by contrast, acetylcholine appeared as bursts rather than dips, and coincident dopamine predicted the vigor of upcoming movements without evidence for persistent plasticity. This implies that local cholinergic timing can demix multiplexed dopamine into at least two downstream modes: a plasticity-promoting teaching signal and a transient performance/vigor signal. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

A further possibility is that cholinergic signals are not merely gates placed downstream of dopamine; in some striatal territories they may carry error-like content of their own. During Pavlovian learning and extinction, anterior dorsal striatal acetylcholine exhibited phase-specific prediction-error structure, with positive and negative RPEs expressed in different parts of the ACh waveform, and silencing local ACh release impaired extinction while sparing initial acquisition 8. In reversal settings, dorsal striatal ACh elevations following unexpected non-reward were causally required for behavioral adaptation 9. These findings fit naturally with the view that cholinergic circuitry is especially important for negative updating, extinction, and contingency revision–precisely the situations in which cached action values must be weakened rather than strengthened. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

At the same time, the dopamine–acetylcholine relationship is not a single canonical anti-phase motif repeated everywhere. In ventrolateral striatum, dopamine inhibits acetylcholine transients through CIN D2 receptors, while cortical and thalamic glutamatergic inputs are required to drive acetylcholine release in the first place 10. In nucleus accumbens, dopamine–acetylcholine correlations vary across task phases rather than obeying one fixed relationship 11. And across striatal subregions, the alignment between CIN pauses and dopamine RPEs can diverge sharply, with ventral striatum even showing reward-cue-related increases in both signals rather than a simple pause-plus-burst pattern 12. Thus, cholinergic modulation should be treated as a regionally parameterized local controller, not a universal scalar opponent to dopamine. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Taken together, the computational picture is now much richer than “dopamine computes the error, acetylcholine sets general arousal.” A better approximation is that dopamine carries a candidate teaching signal into striatum, and cholinergic circuitry then finalizes its local instructional form: it gates when dopamine becomes plasticity-relevant, rescales terminal release according to current context, helps separate learning from performance-related dopamine, and in some territories contributes its own opponent signal for extinction and behavioral flexibility 7, 10, 8. In reinforcement-learning terms, acetylcholine is not the loss itself and not the canonical TD error either; it is better understood as a fast, state-dependent eligibility and gain controller that determines where, when, and in what effective sign that error is allowed to modify corticostriatal policy. A recent computational model is broadly consonant with this interpretation, showing that cholinergic pauses can solve a structural credit-assignment problem by restricting plasticity to the channels active around action selection 13.
